newsitem.title: JAPAN: Kohl says Germany can meet Maastricht criteria.
newsitem.headline: Kohl says Germany can meet Maastricht criteria.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, under attack for his financial policies, said in Tokyo on Friday the country can meet the Maastricht criteria in 1997 for Europe's planned single currency.
"We will achieve the Maastricht criteria, though that will not be easy," Kohl told a news conference.

Referring to a report by the country's six leading economic institutes, which predicted Germany would not meet the tough criteria for economic and monetary union (EMU), Kohl said: "I think the forecast is wrong."

However Kohl, who on Thursday broke Konrad Adenauer's record as Germany's longest-serving chancellor this century, admitted the 1997 budget needed to be very carefully drafted and said some fundamental reforms were necessary.

Kohl was closely questioned about remarks in an emergency parliamentary debate on Wednesday by Finance Minister Theo Waigel, who admitted that his 1997 budget shortfall was even bigger than previously stated.

Some deputies, who had accompanied Kohl on his Asian tour to promote German business interests in the fast-growing region, had to rush back to Bonn earlier this week as the government came under attack over its 1997 budget.
But Kohl gave no details on how the EMU criteria would be met and also declined to comment on France's plan to use 37.5 billion francs ($7.35 billion) in pension funds to cut its 1997 budget deficit.
The plan was accepted by the European Commission on Thursday but sparked fears that other European Union countries struggling to meet tough criteria for economic and monetary union would follow suit.
Earlier on Friday, Ernst Welteke, a member of the Bundesbank council, said in Singapore that Germany was not satisfied with the moves made by France so far to meet convergence criteria.

"The new currency needs confidence. And if they do some tricks in the upcoming member states, it's not very good for the public. The public will not have enough confidence in the stability of the new currency," he said.
Kohl, who arrived in Tokyo on Thursday on the last leg of an Asian tour, also played salesman for Deutsche Telekom shares in Tokyo ahead of its flotation later this month.

"I will try to help so that also my friend, the Japanese prime minister, will buy Telekom shares in a few weeks. That will be a good investment," Kohl said, following a meeting with Ryutaro Hashimoto, Japan's 10th prime minister since the German politician took office in 1982.
Their talks took place while the German telecom giant held a roadshow in Tokyo ahead of Europe's biggest-ever flotation on November 18. A part of its 500 million shares will be traded in Tokyo.

Kohl and Hashimoto agreed to hold summits every year to bolster ties between the two countries. The next meeting is scheduled for June in Denver where the G-7 meeting of industrialised nations will take place.
Hashimoto said Japan hoped to see substantial progress in its talks with Bonn over environment and pensions by then. Tokyo invited German President Roman Herzog to Japan in April.

Together with German business leaders, including Telekom's management board chairman Ron Sommer, Kohl visited the Tokyo Stock Exchange where the chancellor won applause and brought trading to a halt for a few minutes.
